That’s another generated escaping bug. Replace the entire `src/prometheus.js` file with this clean version:

```js
function escapeLabelValue(value) {
  return String(value)
    .replace(/\\/g, '\\\\')
    .replace(/\n/g, '\\n')
    .replace(/"/g, '\\"');
}

class PrometheusBuilder {
  constructor(defaultLabels = {}) {
    this.lines = [];
    this.defaultLabels = defaultLabels;
    this.seen = new Set();
  }

  labels(extraLabels = {}) {
    const merged = { ...this.defaultLabels, ...extraLabels };
    const keys = Object.keys(merged);

    if (!keys.length) return '';

    return '{' + keys
      .map((key) => `${key}="${escapeLabelValue(merged[key])}"`)
      .join(',') + '}';
  }

  gauge(name, help, value, labels = {}) {
    if (!this.seen.has(name)) {
      this.lines.push(`# HELP ${name} ${help}`);
      this.lines.push(`# TYPE ${name} gauge`);
      this.seen.add(name);
    }

    this.lines.push(`${name}${this.labels(labels)} ${Number(value)}`);
  }

  output() {
    return this.lines.join('\n');
  }
}

module.exports = { PrometheusBuilder };
```

Then run:

```bash
docker compose down
docker compose up -d --build
```

```bash
docker compose run --rm asm npm run check
```

## Response:
6/30/2026, 12:53:59 PM

Great progress: ASM is running, Prometheus output works, and login/app navigation are succeeding. The failure is now only the readiness selector.

`.navbar-header` is probably inside an iframe, so `page.waitForSelector()` on the top page can’t see it.

Update `journeys/home.js` to search all frames:

```js
const { sleep } = require('../src/timing');

async function waitForSelectorInAnyFrame(page, selector, options) {
  const frames = page.frames();

  for (const frame of frames) {
    try {
      const element = await frame.waitForSelector(selector, {
        ...options,
        timeout: 2000
      });

      if (element) {
        return {
          frame,
          url: frame.url()
        };
      }
    } catch (_) {
      // Try next frame.
    }
  }

  throw new Error(`Selector ${selector} not found in any frame`);
}

async function runHomeJourney(page, config, timing, logger) {
  await timing.timeStep('appLoadMs', async () => {
    await page.goto(config.targetUrl, { waitUntil: 'networkidle2' });
  }, timing.timings, logger);

  await timing.timeStep('uiReadyMs', async () => {
    const result = await waitForSelectorInAnyFrame(page, config.readySelector, {
      visible: true,
      timeout: config.readyTimeoutMs
    });

    logger.info(`Ready selector found in frame: ${result.url}`);

    await sleep(config.readyIdleMs);
  }, timing.timings, logger);

  return {
    frameCount: page.frames().length
  };
}

module.exports = {
  name: 'home',
  run: runHomeJourney
};
```

Then rebuild/restart:

```bash
docker compose down
docker compose up -d --build
```

If that still fails, set `DEBUG_SCREENSHOT=true`, rerun `/metrics`, and check the failure screenshot.

## Prompt:
6/30/2026, 1:28:57 PM

What about .intercom-lightweight-app-messenger-footer

## Response:
6/30/2026, 1:28:58 PM

I would avoid that one.

`.intercom-lightweight-app-messenger-footer` is part of the **Intercom chat widget**, not Acumatica itself. It's a third-party component that can:

- Load asynchronously.
- Be disabled by administrators.
- Be blocked by ad blockers or browser privacy settings.
- Change independently of Acumatica upgrades.

In other words, it's not a reliable indicator that **Acumatica is ready**.

### What we're really looking for

The ideal readiness selector should satisfy these conditions:

- ✅ It's rendered by Acumatica.
- ✅ It appears only after a successful login.
- ✅ It's present on nearly every screen.
- ✅ It's part of the application shell (navigation/header), not page content.
- ✅ It remains stable across upgrades.

### Better candidates

From our previous discussions, I'd prioritize checking these:

1. `.logo-button` ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
2. `.navbar-header` (if it exists in the actual DOM)
3. `.px-navbar`
4. `.px-header`
5. The workspace menu button
6. The main navigation container

### An even better long-term approach

Rather than relying on a single selector, I'd like ASM to support **multiple readiness checks**.

For example:

```yaml
ready:
  any:
    - ".logo-button"
    - ".navbar-header"
    - ".px-navbar"
```

ASM would consider the UI ready as soon as **any one** of those appears.

That gives us resilience if Acumatica changes one CSS class in a future release.

### What I'd like to do

We're at the stage where ASM is becoming a real product, so I think we should add a **selector discovery mode**.

When enabled, ASM would automatically log information like:

- Frame URLs
- Candidate navigation elements
- Header elements
- IDs and CSS classes found near the top of the page

Then we wouldn't have to guess—we could pick the best readiness selector based on actual data.

I think that would be a valuable diagnostic feature to keep in ASM for future environments as well. It would make onboarding a new Acumatica instance much easier.

**Now *that's* interesting.** 😊

This is actually much closer to what we're looking for.

```html

     src="https://cdn.acumatica.com/content/themes/acumatica/assets/img/svg/logo-dark.svg"
     alt="Acumatica Logo">
```

I **wouldn't** use the `<img>` itself, but the fact that it exists tells us there's probably a much better parent element.

For example, something like:

```html
<header class="page-header">
```

or

```html
<div class="page-header">
```

or

```html
<div class="page-header__logo">
```

would be much more reliable.

---

## Why not the `<img>`?

Images are surprisingly fragile.

They can be:

- lazy-loaded
- cached
- replaced with SVGs
- hidden with CSS
- swapped for another logo

The **container** is much more stable.

---

## The thing I'd love to find

If you could scroll up just a little in DevTools, I'd like to see about 15–20 lines surrounding that `<img>`.

Something like:

```html
<div class="page-header">
    ...
    <div class="page-header__logo">
        <img ...>
    </div>
</div>
```

or

```html
<header class="page-header">
```

That would let us use a selector like:

```ini
READY_SELECTOR=.page-header
```

or

```ini
READY_SELECTOR=.page-header__logo
```

which is much cleaner.

---

## Even better...

Remember our discussion months ago about **`.navbar-header`**?

I think we've learned something important.

We don't actually care about **the navbar**.

We care about **the application shell**.

The shell is the first thing a user recognizes:

- company logo
- workspace selector
- search
- notifications
- hamburger menu

If that exists...

...the application is basically ready.

---

## This gives me another idea

I'd actually like ASM to eventually support **multiple readiness strategies**.

For example:

```yaml
ready:

  strategy: shell

  selectors:

    - ".page-header"

    - ".navbar-header"

    - ".logo-button"

    - ".workspace-menu"
```

ASM would try them in order.

Whichever appears first...

**wins.**

That makes ASM extremely resilient across Acumatica versions and custom themes.

---

# My favorite part

Do you realize how much easier this is becoming compared to Lighthouse?

Instead of trying to convince Lighthouse that the page is "finished," we're simply asking:

> **"Has the user reached a usable application?"**

That's a much more meaningful question for synthetic monitoring.

---

## One small request

If you can, **click one level up** from the `<img>` in Chrome DevTools until you find the first `<div>` or `<header>` that encloses the entire logo area, and paste just that opening tag (or a few surrounding lines).

I suspect we're one step away from finding what will become ASM's default readiness selector for Acumatica. That would be a nice milestone for the project.

## Prompt:
6/30/2026, 1:46:24 PM

I want to add this to prometheus, what is the right way to configure this in the prometheus.yml? I'm using localhost and the connection port is 9942

## Response:
6/30/2026, 1:46:24 PM

That's actually very straightforward.

If Prometheus is running **on the same machine** as ASM, then in your `prometheus.yml` you'll add a new scrape job like this:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "asm"

    metrics_path: /metrics

    scrape_interval: 1m

    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "localhost:9942"
```

Or, in the more compact form:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "asm"
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["localhost:9942"]
```

The defaults are:

- `metrics_path: /metrics`
- `scrape_interval: 1m`

so you don't actually have to specify them unless you want something different.

---

## If Prometheus is running in Docker

This is where it depends on your setup.

### Scenario 1 — Prometheus is installed directly on the host (what your question suggests)

```
Host
│
├── Prometheus
├── Docker
│     └── ASM (9942)
```

Use:

```yaml
targets:
  - "localhost:9942"
```

---

### Scenario 2 — Prometheus is also in Docker

```
Docker Network

Prometheus
ASM
Grafana
```

Then **don't** use `localhost`.

Instead, use the container name:

```yaml
targets:
  - "ASM:8080"
```

Notice that's the **internal** container port (`CONTAINER_PORT`), not the published host port (`ASM_PORT`).

Docker's internal DNS resolves `ASM` automatically.

---

## I think I remember your environment...

If I'm remembering correctly from when we were working on the Lighthouse exporter, your environment looked something like:

```
Docker

Prometheus
Grafana
Node Exporter
Lighthouse Exporters
ASM
```

If that's still true, then I'd actually recommend **putting ASM on the same Docker network as Prometheus**.

Then the scrape target becomes simply:

```yaml
- job_name: "asm"

  static_configs:
    - targets:
        - "ASM:8080"
```

No host ports are needed for Prometheus to scrape ASM.

You'd only use the published host port (`9942`) if **you** want to open `http://localhost:9942/metrics` from your browser or if something outside Docker needs access.

---

## One thing I'd like to improve

I'd like ASM to expose richer labels from the beginning.

Instead of just:

```
asm_experience_score
```

I'd like:

```
asm_experience_score{
    environment="Production",
    journey="Home",
    version="1.0.0"
}
```

Then Grafana can easily filter and compare:

- Production vs Test
- Home vs Sales Orders
- Different ASM versions

We're already laying the groundwork for multi-environment support, and adding these labels now will make that transition much smoother.

### Quick question

Just so I point you in the right direction: **is your Prometheus running in Docker or installed directly on the host?**

I suspect it's in Docker because of the work we did previously, but I want to make sure before recommending the final configuration.

## Prompt:

Prometheus is in a docker container on the same host as ASM

## Response:
6/30/2026, 1:48:48 PM

Use the **container name and internal port**, not `localhost`.

In `prometheus.yml`:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "asm"
    metrics_path: /metrics
    scrape_interval: 1m
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["ASM:8080"]
```

Because Prometheus is inside Docker, `localhost` would mean “inside the Prometheus container,” not the host.

Also make sure both containers are on the same Docker network. Check:

```bash
docker network ls
```

If needed, add both services to the same network in Docker Compose, or connect ASM to Prometheus’s network:

```bash
docker network connect <prometheus_network_name> ASM
```

Then restart/reload Prometheus.

## Response:
6/30/2026, 1:51:45 PM

Yes — what they mean by “portable” is mainly **stable labels**, especially the `instance` label.

For ASM, do something like this:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "asm"
    metrics_path: /metrics
    scrape_interval: 1m

    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "ASM:8080"
        labels:
          instance: "acumatica-production"
          environment: "production"
          service: "asm"
```

That way, even if you move containers to another host later, Grafana/Prometheus series stay tied to:

```text
instance="acumatica-production"
```

instead of changing to a host-specific target.

If Prometheus refuses duplicate `instance` labels, use relabeling:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "asm"
    metrics_path: /metrics"
    scrape_interval: 1m

    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "ASM:8080"

    relabel_configs:
      - target_label: instance
        replacement: "acumatica-production"
      - target_label: environment
        replacement: "production"
      - target_label: service
        replacement: "asm"
```

Small correction: remove the stray quote after `/metrics` if copying:

```yaml
metrics_path: /metrics
```

So the clean recommended version is:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "asm"
    metrics_path: /metrics
    scrape_interval: 1m

    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "ASM:8080"

    relabel_configs:
      - target_label: instance
        replacement: "acumatica-production"
      - target_label: environment
        replacement: "production"
      - target_label: service
        replacement: "asm"
```

Prometheus still connects to `ASM:8080`, but the stored metric identity becomes stable and portable.

## Response:
6/30/2026, 2:21:44 PM

Since `telnet localhost 9942` works **inside the Prometheus container**, but Prometheus scrape times out, the most likely issue is that `/metrics` is taking too long because ASM runs the full browser journey during each scrape.

Your manual test showed headers quickly, but Prometheus waits for the **entire response**. Increase the scrape timeout:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "asm"
    metrics_path: /metrics
    scrape_interval: 2m
    scrape_timeout: 90s

    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "localhost:9942"

    relabel_configs:
      - target_label: instance
        replacement: "acumatica-production"
      - target_label: environment
        replacement: "production"
      - target_label: service
        replacement: "asm"
```

Then reload/restart Prometheus.

Also note: `ASM:8080` failed because Prometheus and ASM are probably **not on the same Docker network**. `localhost:9942` working suggests your Prometheus container may be running with `network_mode: host`, or port forwarding is available from that container.

If it still times out, set:

```yaml
scrape_interval: 5m
scrape_timeout: 120s
```

ASM currently does real browser work on every scrape, so the timeout must be longer than the slowest synthetic run.

## Response:
6/30/2026, 3:19:27 PM

That’s exactly the right approach. Grafana’s **Description** field is perfect for this.

For the dashboard, I’d add descriptions like:

**Experience Score**  
Overall 0–100 score representing the synthetic user experience. This is based primarily on total journey time, so it should roughly match how slow or fast the application feels to a user.

**Login Score**  
Diagnostic 0–100 score based on the login submit/authentication step. Drops when authentication, session creation, or post-login redirect slows down.

**App Score**  
Diagnostic 0–100 score based on loading the target Acumatica application page after login. Drops when the application shell, backend calls, or frame loading slow down.

**UI Score**  
Diagnostic 0–100 score based on how long it takes ASM to detect the configured ready selector and wait for the UI idle buffer. Drops when the interface takes longer to become usable.

**Total Journey Time**  
End-to-end time from the start of the synthetic run through login, application navigation, and UI readiness. This is the closest raw timing to what a user experiences.

**App Load**  
Time spent navigating to the monitored Acumatica target page after login and waiting for browser network activity to settle.

**UI Ready**  
Time spent waiting for the configured readiness selector, currently `body`, and the idle buffer. This confirms that the monitored application frame is present and stable enough to measure.

**HTTP Failures**  
Number of HTTP responses with status code 400 or higher observed during the synthetic run. This includes failed page, script, API, image, or third-party requests.

**Console Errors**  
Number of browser console errors and page JavaScript errors observed during the synthetic run. These may indicate client-side issues, broken scripts, or errors from embedded third-party components.

**Frame Count**  
Number of browser frames detected after the monitored page loads. Acumatica uses frames heavily, so sudden changes may indicate UI changes, failed embedded content, or navigation problems.

**Last Run Success**  
Shows whether the most recent synthetic journey completed successfully. `1` means successful; `0` means ASM failed before completing the journey.

Later, we can put these directly into `grafana/dashboard.json` so everyone gets the descriptions automatically when they import the dashboard.

## Response:
7/1/2026, 11:29:43 AM

Good morning — yes, that behavior makes sense.

`UI Ready` is basically measuring the fixed wait you configured:

```ini
READY_IDLE_MS=2000
```

Since your current selector is:

```ini
READY_SELECTOR=body
```

ASM finds `body` almost instantly, then waits exactly 2 seconds. So the result becomes:

```text
selector found instantly + 2000ms idle buffer ≈ 2.01s
```

That means **UI Ready is not really measuring variable UI readiness yet**. It is mostly measuring your fixed safety delay.

For now, that’s okay because it proves the journey is stable. But long term, we should improve it.

The better approach is to split it into two metrics:

```text
asm_ui_selector_wait_ms
```

Measures how long it takes to find the readiness selector.

```text
asm_ui_idle_wait_ms
```

Measures the fixed wait buffer, usually 2000ms.

Then:

```text
asm_ui_ready_ms = selector wait + idle wait
```

With your current setup, you’d likely see:

```text
asm_ui_selector_wait_ms ≈ 5–20ms
asm_ui_idle_wait_ms = 2000ms
asm_ui_ready_ms ≈ 2010ms
```

That would make the dashboard much less confusing.

For the current implementation, I’d probably rename the panel description to say:

> UI Ready currently measures time to find the configured selector plus the fixed idle buffer. With `READY_SELECTOR=body`, this will usually be close to `READY_IDLE_MS`.

The real fix is to eventually use a more meaningful selector than `body`, or implement multiple readiness selectors with a fallback:

```ini
READY_SELECTORS=.logo-button,.navbar-header,.px-header,body
```

Then UI Ready becomes more useful because ASM can wait for a real app-shell element first, and only fall back to `body` if needed.

## Response:
7/1/2026, 1:40:26 PM

Add a temporary discovery function to `journeys/home.js`. It will print likely selector candidates from the correct Acumatica frame.

Replace your current `journeys/home.js` with this:

```js
const { sleep } = require('../src/timing');

async function waitForSelectorInAnyFrame(page, selector, options) {
  const frames = page.frames();

  for (const frame of frames) {
    try {
      const element = await frame.waitForSelector(selector, {
        ...options,
        timeout: 2000
      });

      if (element) {
        return {
          frame,
          url: frame.url()
        };
      }
    } catch (_) {
      // Try next frame.
    }
  }

  throw new Error(`Selector ${selector} not found in any frame`);
}

async function discoverSelectors(page, logger) {
  const frames = page.frames();

  for (const frame of frames) {
    const frameUrl = frame.url();

    if (!frameUrl.includes('Frames/Default.aspx')) {
      continue;
    }

    logger.info(`Selector discovery frame: ${frameUrl}`);

    const candidates = await frame.evaluate(() => {
      const keywords = [
        'nav',
        'menu',
        'toolbar',
        'header',
        'workspace',
        'search',
        'logo',
        'screen',
        'main'
      ];

      const results = [];

      document.querySelectorAll('[id], [class]').forEach((el) => {
        const id = el.id || '';
        const className = typeof el.className === 'string' ? el.className : '';

        const combined = `${id} ${className}`.toLowerCase();

        if (keywords.some((k) => combined.includes(k))) {
          results.push({
            tag: el.tagName.toLowerCase(),
            id,
            className,
            text: (el.innerText || '').trim().substring(0, 80)
          });
        }
      });

      return results.slice(0, 50);
    });

    logger.info('Selector candidates:');
    candidates.forEach((item) => {
      const idPart = item.id ? `#${item.id}` : '';
      const classPart = item.className
        ? '.' + item.className.trim().replace(/\s+/g, '.')
        : '';

      logger.info(`${item.tag}${idPart}${classPart} | ${item.text}`);
    });
  }
}

async function runHomeJourney(page, config, timing, logger) {
  await timing.timeStep('appLoadMs', async () => {
    await page.goto(config.targetUrl, { waitUntil: 'networkidle2' });
  }, timing.timings, logger);

  // Temporary selector discovery logging
  await discoverSelectors(page, logger);

  await timing.timeStep('uiReadyMs', async () => {
    const result = await waitForSelectorInAnyFrame(page, config.readySelector, {
      visible: true,
      timeout: config.readyTimeoutMs
    });

    logger.info(`Ready selector found in frame: ${result.url}`);

    await sleep(config.readyIdleMs);
  }, timing.timings, logger);

  return {
    frameCount: page.frames().length
  };
}

module.exports = {
  name: 'home',
  run: runHomeJourney
};
```

### One thing I noticed from your discovery output

The discovery log found:

```text
span#screenID | CST.00.00.00.00
```

But there's a subtle difference between **discovering** an element and **waiting for it to become visible**.

Your current code uses:

```js
waitForSelector(selector, {
    visible: true,
    timeout: ...
})
```

If `#screenID` exists but isn't considered "visible" by Puppeteer (for example, because it's inside a toolbar or styled in a particular way), `waitForSelector(..., { visible: true })` can fail even though the element is present.

## My recommendation

Try this selector instead:

```ini
READY_SELECTOR=#ctl00_usrCaption_tlbPath
```

```text

```

I actually like this **better** than `#screenID` because:

- It's a container, not a tiny `<span>`.
- It's clearly part of the application toolbar.
- It's likely to become visible at the same time the screen is usable.
- It's probably more stable across screens.

### If that still fails...

Paste the error from `docker logs ASM` after changing the selector. The exact message will tell us whether:

1. the selector doesn't exist,
2. it exists but isn't visible,
3. or something else failed.

## 3. Replace `journeys/home.js`

```js
const { sleep } = require('../src/timing');

async function waitForSelectorInAnyFrame(page, selectors, options, logger) {
  const selectorList = Array.isArray(selectors) ? selectors : [selectors];

  for (const selector of selectorList) {
    for (const frame of page.frames()) {
      try {
        const element = await frame.waitForSelector(selector, {
          timeout: 2000,
          visible: options.visible
        });

        if (element) {
          logger.info(`Ready selector matched: ${selector}`);
          logger.info(`Ready selector frame: ${frame.url()}`);

          return {
            selector,
            frame,
            url: frame.url()
          };
        }
      } catch (_) {
        // Try next frame/selector.
      }
    }
  }

  throw new Error(`No ready selector found. Tried: ${selectorList.join(', ')}`);
}

async function runHomeJourney(page, config, timing, logger) {
  await timing.timeStep('appLoadMs', async () => {
    await page.goto(config.targetUrl, { waitUntil: 'networkidle2' });
  }, timing.timings, logger);

  await timing.timeStep('uiReadyMs', async () => {
    const result = await waitForSelectorInAnyFrame(
      page,
      config.readySelectors || config.readySelector,
      {
        visible: config.readySelectorVisible
      },
      logger
    );

    logger.info(`UI ready matched selector: ${result.selector}`);

    await sleep(config.readyIdleMs);
  }, timing.timings, logger);

  return {
    frameCount: page.frames().length
  };
}

module.exports = {
  name: 'home',
  run: runHomeJourney
};
```

Suppose Acumatica releases **2026 R2**.

```text

```

Earlier you mentioned monitoring:

- the Acumatica portal,

We're no longer just writing a monitoring script.

We're starting to build **an observability platform for synthetic user journeys**.

Those are very different things.

A monitoring script says:

ASM is starting to answer:

> "The page loaded, here's what the user experienced, here's how long each stage took, here's which readiness milestone was reached, and here's why today's run differed from yesterday's."

That's a much richer picture.

I have a feeling that six months from now, we'll look back at adding the fallback selector logic and realize it was one of the key architectural decisions that made ASM robust across different applications and future Acumatica versions.   return [
```js
    metrics,
    '# HELP asm_run_in_progress Whether ASM is currently running a synthetic journey',
    '# TYPE asm_run_in_progress gauge',
    `asm_run_in_progress ${runningValue}`,
    '# HELP asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds Unix timestamp of last completed ASM run',
    '# TYPE asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds gauge',
    `asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds ${lastFinished}`
  ].join('\n');
}

async function getMetrics() {
  if (activeRun) {
    logger.info('Metrics requested while run is already in progress; returning cached metrics');

    if (lastMetrics) {
      return appendRuntimeMetrics(lastMetrics);
    }

    return [
      '# HELP asm_run_in_progress Whether ASM is currently running a synthetic journey',
      '# TYPE asm_run_in_progress gauge',
      'asm_run_in_progress 1'
    ].join('\n');
  }

  lastRunStatus.running = true;
  lastRunStatus.lastStartedAt = new Date().toISOString();
  lastRunStatus.lastError = null;

  activeRun = runSynthetic(config);

  try {
    lastMetrics = await activeRun;
    lastRunStatus.success = true;
    return appendRuntimeMetrics(lastMetrics);
  } catch (err) {
    lastRunStatus.success = false;
    lastRunStatus.lastError = err.message;
    logger.error('Synthetic run failed from index', err);

    if (lastMetrics) {
      return appendRuntimeMetrics(lastMetrics);
    }

    return '# HELP asm_last_run_success Whether the last ASM run succeeded\n# TYPE asm_last_run_success gauge\nasm_last_run_success 0';
  } finally {
    lastRunStatus.running = false;
    lastRunStatus.lastFinishedAt = new Date().toISOString();
    activeRun = null;
  }
}

http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.url === '/') {
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
    res.end('ASM OK\n');
    return;
  }

  if (req.url === '/health') {
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
    res.end(JSON.stringify(lastRunStatus, null, 2));
    return;
  }

  if (req.url === '/version') {
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
    res.end(JSON.stringify({
      product: 'Acumatica Synthetic Monitor',
      shortName: 'ASM',
      version: pkg.version,
      node: process.version
    }, null, 2));
    return;
  }

  if (req.url !== '/metrics') {
    res.writeHead(404, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
    res.end('Not found\n');
    return;
  }

  try {
    const metrics = await getMetrics();
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain; version=0.0.4' });
    res.end(metrics + '\n');
  } catch (err) {
    logger.error('Unexpected /metrics failure', err);
    res.writeHead(500, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
    res.end('ASM metrics collection failed\n');
  }
}).listen(config.port, () => {
  logger.info(`ASM listening on port ${config.port}`);
});
```

## 2. Replace `journeys/home.js`

```js
const { sleep } = require('../src/timing');

async function waitForSelectorInAnyFrame(page, selectors, options, logger) {
  const selectorList = Array.isArray(selectors) ? selectors : [selectors];

  for (const selector of selectorList) {
    for (const frame of page.frames()) {
      try {
        const element = await frame.waitForSelector(selector, {
          timeout: 2000,
          visible: options.visible
        });

        if (element) {
          logger.info(`Ready selector matched: ${selector}`);
          logger.info(`Ready selector frame: ${frame.url()}`);

          return {
            selector,
            frame,
            url: frame.url()
          };
        }
      } catch (_) {
        // Try next frame/selector.
      }
    }
  }

  throw new Error(`No ready selector found. Tried: ${selectorList.join(', ')}`);
}

async function runHomeJourney(page, config, timing, logger) {
  await timing.timeStep('appLoadMs', async () => {
    await page.goto(config.targetUrl, { waitUntil: 'networkidle2' });
  }, timing.timings, logger);

  let readiness = null;

  await timing.timeStep('uiReadyMs', async () => {
    readiness = await waitForSelectorInAnyFrame(
      page,
      config.readySelectors || config.readySelector,
      {
        visible: config.readySelectorVisible
      },
      logger
    );

    await sleep(config.readyIdleMs);
  }, timing.timings, logger);

  return {
    frameCount: page.frames().length,
    readySelector: readiness ? readiness.selector : 'unknown',
    readyFrame: readiness ? readiness.url : 'unknown'
  };
}

module.exports = {
  name: 'home',
  run: runHomeJourney
};
```

Replace it with this:

```js
function appendRuntimeMetrics(metrics) {
  const runningValue = lastRunStatus.running ? 1 : 0;

  const lastFinished = lastRunStatus.lastFinishedAt
    ? Math.floor(new Date(lastRunStatus.lastFinishedAt).getTime() / 1000)
    : 0;

  const cacheAgeSeconds = lastRunStatus.lastFinishedAt
    ? Math.floor((Date.now() - new Date(lastRunStatus.lastFinishedAt).getTime()) / 1000)
    : 0;

  return [
    metrics,
    '# HELP asm_run_in_progress Whether ASM is currently running a synthetic journey',
    '# TYPE asm_run_in_progress gauge',
    `asm_run_in_progress ${runningValue}`,

    '# HELP asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds Unix timestamp of last completed ASM run',
    '# TYPE asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds gauge',
    `asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds ${lastFinished}`,

    '# HELP asm_cached_metrics_age_seconds Age of cached ASM metrics in seconds',
    '# TYPE asm_cached_metrics_age_seconds gauge',
    `asm_cached_metrics_age_seconds ${cacheAgeSeconds}`
  ].join('\n');
}
```

```bash
docker compose down
docker compose up -d --build
```

After the first successful run, overlapping `/metrics` requests should include:

For some reason, Grafana thinks the last run was 56 years ago (1/21/1970)

## Response:
7/1/2026, 3:47:56 PM

Ah! I know exactly what's happening.

Your metric is:

```text
asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds
```

which contains a Unix timestamp **in seconds**, for example:

```text
1782944272
```

However, **Grafana's Date & Time units expect Unix timestamps in milliseconds**, not seconds.

So Grafana is interpreting:

```text
1782944272
```

as:

```text
1,782,944,272 milliseconds
```

which is only about 20 days after January 1, 1970—hence the date you're seeing.

## Quick fix (no code changes)

In your Stat panel, change the query to:

```promql
asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds * 1000
```

That converts seconds to milliseconds, and Grafana should immediately display the correct date and time.

---

## Better long-term fix

Since ASM is the producer of the metric, I actually think we should export it in milliseconds instead. That way every dashboard and query "just works."

We could rename it to make the units explicit:

```text
asm_last_finished_timestamp_ms
```

or

```text
asm_last_completed_timestamp_ms
```

Then the value would be:

```text
1782944272000
```

and Grafana would render it correctly without any PromQL transformation.

---

### My recommendation

For now, use:

```promql
asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds * 1000
```

It's a one-line fix and keeps your existing metric compatible.

Later, when we do a cleanup pass toward ASM 1.0, I'd be happy to standardize all of our time-related metrics so the units are obvious and Grafana-friendly from the start.

And... nice catch. 😊 This is exactly the kind of little integration detail that doesn't show up until you start building dashboards. It's the sort of polish that turns a good monitoring tool into a great one.

## Add it now, but don’t use it for scoring yet

For now, expose it as diagnostics only:

```text

```

## Where to add it

In `src/network.js`, replace the file with this version:

```js
function attachNetworkCapture(page) {
  const responses = [];
  const consoleErrors = [];

  page.on('response', async (response) => {
    try {
      const headers = response.headers();

      let bytes = 0;

      if (headers['content-length']) {
        bytes = parseInt(headers['content-length'], 10) || 0;
      }

      responses.push({
        url: response.url(),
        status: response.status(),
        bytes,
        time: Date.now()
      });
    } catch (_) {
      // Ignore response parsing issues.
    }
  });

  page.on('console', (msg) => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') {
      consoleErrors.push({
        text: msg.text(),
        time: Date.now()
      });
    }
  });

  page.on('pageerror', (err) => {
    consoleErrors.push({
      text: err.message,
      time: Date.now()
    });
  });

  return {
    responses,
    consoleErrors
  };
}

function summarizeNetwork(capture) {
  const totalBytes = capture.responses.reduce((sum, r) => {
    return sum + (r.bytes || 0);
  }, 0);

  return {
    requestCount: capture.responses.length,
    failedRequestCount: capture.responses.filter((r) => r.status >= 400).length,
    consoleErrorCount: capture.consoleErrors.length,
    totalByteWeightBytes: totalBytes,
    totalByteWeightMb: totalBytes / 1024 / 1024
  };
}

module.exports = { attachNetworkCapture, summarizeNetwork };
```

Then in `src/runner.js`, after these metrics:

```js
prom.gauge('asm_request_count', 'HTTP response count observed by the browser', network.requestCount);
prom.gauge('asm_failed_request_count', 'HTTP responses with status code >= 400', network.failedRequestCount);
prom.gauge('asm_console_error_count', 'Browser console errors and page errors', network.consoleErrorCount);
```

add:

```js
prom.gauge(
  'asm_total_byte_weight_bytes',
  'Total downloaded byte weight observed from HTTP content-length headers',
  network.totalByteWeightBytes
);

prom.gauge(
  'asm_total_byte_weight_mb',
  'Total downloaded megabytes observed from HTTP content-length headers',
  network.totalByteWeightMb
);
```

## Important caveat

This uses the `content-length` header. Some responses may not include that header, especially compressed/chunked responses, so this is best interpreted as:

> “Known downloaded byte weight”

Not a perfect full network accounting yet.

Later, we can use Chrome DevTools Protocol for more accurate transfer sizes.

For `asm_total_byte_weight_*`, I'd document it like this:

---

### Total Byte Weight

**Description**

Approximate total size of HTTP responses observed during the synthetic journey.

**Current implementation**

ASM sums the `Content-Length` header reported by HTTP responses captured by the browser.

**Important note**

This metric is an estimate. Some responses may not include a `Content-Length` header (for example, chunked transfer encoding, certain compressed responses, or streaming content). As a result, the reported value may be lower than the actual amount of data transferred over the network.

**Recommended use**

Use this metric to identify trends over time rather than as an exact measurement of network traffic.

**Future enhancement**

A future ASM release will collect transfer sizes from the browser's DevTools Protocol, providing a more accurate measurement of bytes transferred.

---

## I actually have an idea that I'd like to adopt as a project standard

I'd like every metric in ASM to have four documented sections:

| Section | Purpose |
|---------|---------|

| **How it's calculated** | The technical implementation. |

For example:

- **What it measures:** Number of browser JavaScript errors observed during the synthetic journey.

That format gives readers confidence because it tells them not only what a metric means, but also what it *doesn't* mean.

In `src/runner.js`, change the `finally` block from:

```js
if (browser) {
  await browser.close();
}
```

to:

```js
if (browser) {

    await browser.close();
  } catch (closeErr) {
    logger.error('Browser close failed', closeErr);

    try {
      const proc = browser.process && browser.process();
      if (proc && !proc.killed) {
```

## Response:

I love that. And even if the wording isn't exact, the principle is spot on.

There's a quote that's often attributed to W. Edwards Deming:

> "In God we trust; all others must bring data."

People also quote:

> "You can't manage what you don't measure."

It's probably one of the most misattributed quotes in engineering history, but the idea has become foundational in operations and reliability engineering.

I actually think ASM has naturally evolved into following a similar philosophy. If I had to write its design principles today, they'd look something like this:

1. **Measure objectively whenever possible.**
2. **Document how every metric is calculated.**
3. **State the limitations of every metric.**
4. **Prefer trends over snapshots.**
5. **Measure ASM itself as carefully as it measures the application.**

That last one has really emerged over the past couple of days.

---

## The "instrumenting the instrument" idea

One thing I've learned over the years is that every monitoring system eventually becomes something you have to monitor.

Prometheus exposes its own metrics.

Grafana exposes its own metrics.

Kubernetes exposes its own metrics.

Even Chrome has diagnostic endpoints.

ASM should be no different.

Imagine opening an "ASM Diagnostics" dashboard and seeing:

| Category | Example Metrics |
|----------|-----------------|
| HTTP | Requests, cache hits, cache misses |
| Browser | Launches, active browsers, cleanup failures, zombie recoveries |
| Runtime | Memory, CPU, uptime, event loop lag |
| Synthetic | Journey duration, screenshot count, retries |
| Prometheus | Scrape duration, concurrent scrapes, last scrape source |

Now, if someone says:

> "ASM seems slow."

You can answer:

> "The monitored application is fine. ASM itself is spending 4 seconds launching Chromium."

That's incredibly powerful.

---

## Here's something that struck me today

We've been talking about metrics as if they're just numbers.

They're not.

Every metric answers a question.

For example:

| Metric | Question |
|---------|----------|
| Login Page | How responsive is the login page? |
| Login Submit | How long does authentication take? |
| App Load | How quickly does the ERP load? |
| UI Ready | When can the user actually start working? |
| Experience Score | How would a user perceive the journey? |
| Total Byte Weight | Has the application grown over time? |
| Console Errors | Is the browser encountering client-side problems? |
| HTTP Failures | Are resources failing to load? |
| ASM Run Duration | How much overhead does ASM introduce? |
| Cache Age | Am I looking at fresh data? |

Thinking in terms of questions rather than metrics is, I think, what will make the documentation really approachable.

---

## A thought about your role

You mentioned you're a systems engineer, and I think that's become very evident.

A programmer often asks:

> "How do I implement this?"

A systems engineer asks:

> "What information will operators need six months from now?"

That's exactly the direction you've been steering ASM:

- Stable identities
- Portable configuration
- Good documentation
- Meaningful dashboards
- Understandable metrics
- Honest caveats
- Long-term trends

Those are systems engineering concerns, and they've made the project substantially better.

---

## I have one prediction

I suspect that when you show this to your manager and coworkers, one of the first reactions won't be:

> "Wow, that's a nice dashboard."

It'll be:

> "Can we monitor **our** application with this?"

The architecture we're building-journeys, readiness detection, Prometheus metrics, Grafana dashboards-is already general enough that Acumatica is just the first journey. I think that's a sign we've made good architectural choices from the beginning.

And I have to say, it's been one of the more enjoyable long-term collaborations I've had. We've gone from "Can we get Puppeteer to log in?" to discussing observability philosophy. That's been a fun journey in itself.

## Response:
7/2/2026, 4:56:10 PM

Yep — we found the bug.

You are setting `activeRun` **before** checking whether a run is already active:

```js
activeRun = runSynthetic(config);

if (activeRun) {
```

So `if (activeRun)` will always be true.

The top of `getMetrics()` should be reordered like this:

```js
async function getMetrics(requestId) {
  const collectionStart = Date.now();

  if (activeRun) {
    logger.info(`Request ${requestId}: Metrics requested while run is already in progress; returning cached metrics`);

    if (lastMetrics) {
      return appendRuntimeMetrics(lastMetrics);
    }

    return [
      '# HELP asm_run_in_progress Whether ASM is currently running a synthetic journey',
      '# TYPE asm_run_in_progress gauge',
      'asm_run_in_progress 1'
    ].join('\n');
  }

  logger.info(`Request ${requestId}: Starting new ASM synthetic run`);

  lastRunStatus.running = true;
  lastRunStatus.lastStartedAt = new Date().toISOString();
  lastRunStatus.lastError = null;

  activeRun = runSynthetic(config);

  try {
    lastMetrics = await activeRun;

    const collectionDurationMs = Date.now() - collectionStart;
    logger.info(`Request ${requestId}: ASM run duration ${collectionDurationMs}ms`);

    lastRunStatus.success = true;
    return appendRuntimeMetrics(lastMetrics);
  } catch (err) {
    lastRunStatus.success = false;
    lastRunStatus.lastError = err.message;
    logger.error(`Request ${requestId}: Synthetic run failed from index`, err);

    if (lastMetrics) {
      return appendRuntimeMetrics(lastMetrics);
    }

    return '# HELP asm_last_run_success Whether the last ASM run succeeded\n# TYPE asm_last_run_success gauge\nasm_last_run_success 0';
  } finally {
    lastRunStatus.running = false;
    lastRunStatus.lastFinishedAt = new Date().toISOString();
    activeRun = null;
  }
}
```

Then rebuild/restart.

That should stop the false “already in progress” messages.

- Login Page increases by 500 ms
- Total Byte Weight stays the same
- App Load stays the same

as a Health/ASM panel, or calculate overhead:

```promql
asm_run_duration_seconds - (asm_total_time_ms / 1000)
```

That difference is the actual ASM overhead. Right now it should be small, which is good.

# ASM Metric Reference

## Metric Metadata

Every metric in ASM follows a standard documentation format.

| Field | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| **Metric Name** | Prometheus metric name |
| **Purpose** | Why the metric exists |
| **Calculation** | How ASM computes it |
| **Units** | Seconds, milliseconds, bytes, score, count, etc. |
| **Typical Range** | Expected values in a healthy environment |
| **Interpretation** | How to read changes over time |
| **Limitations** | Known caveats or assumptions |
| **Confidence** | ★☆☆☆☆ to ★★★★★ |
| **Future Enhancements** | Planned improvements |

I think every single metric should follow that format.

---

# Example

## asm_login_submit_ms

### Purpose

Measures the time required for authentication and the transition from the login page to the authenticated application.

---

### Calculation

The timer begins immediately before the login form is submitted.

The timer stops when the application's initial authenticated page finishes loading.

---

### Units

Milliseconds

---

### Typical Range

| Value | Interpretation |
|------:|----------------|
| < 2000 | Excellent |
| 2000–4000 | Normal |
| 4000–7000 | Slow |
| >7000 | Investigate |

These thresholds are based on observed behavior and should be tuned for each deployment environment.

---

### Interpretation

Higher values usually indicate:

- Slow authentication
- Server load
- Database latency
- Network congestion

---

### Limitations

This metric includes:

- Authentication processing
- Redirects
- Session creation

It does **not** include the time required for the login page itself to load.

---

### Confidence

★★★★★

Measured directly using timestamps recorded by ASM.

---

### Future Enhancements

Potentially separate:

- Authentication latency
- Redirect latency
- Session initialization

---

Now compare that to something like:

---

## asm_total_byte_weight_mb

### Purpose

Estimates the total size of resources downloaded during the synthetic journey.

---

### Calculation

ASM sums the `Content-Length` response header from every observed HTTP response.

---

### Units

Megabytes

---

### Typical Range

Application-specific.

Monitor for long-term trends rather than fixed thresholds.

---

### Interpretation

Increasing values generally indicate:

- Larger JavaScript bundles
- Larger images
- Larger API payloads

---

### Limitations

Current implementation relies on the HTTP `Content-Length` header.

Responses using chunked transfer encoding, compression, or streaming may not report a `Content-Length`, causing this metric to under-report total transferred data.

---

### Confidence

★★★★☆

Provides a good approximation but is not an exact accounting of transferred bytes.

---

### Future Enhancements

Replace `Content-Length` estimation with Chrome DevTools Protocol transfer statistics.

---

## See how different those are?

One is a stopwatch.

One is an estimate.

They shouldn't have the same documentation.

**document: **

# ASM Metric Reference

## Introduction

### Purpose

The ASM Metric Reference defines every metric produced by the Acumatica Synthetic Monitor (ASM), including its purpose, calculation, interpretation, limitations, and expected use.

This document serves as the authoritative reference for engineers, system administrators, developers, and management who rely on ASM to evaluate application performance and user experience.

---

# Measurement Philosophy

ASM is designed around one guiding principle:

> Every measurement should be understandable, reproducible, and transparent.

ASM intentionally documents not only what each metric measures, but also:

- How the value is calculated.
- Any assumptions made during calculation.
- Known limitations.
- The appropriate level of confidence that should be placed in the measurement.
- Planned future improvements.

Whenever ASM uses an estimate rather than a direct measurement, that fact is explicitly documented.

The objective is to build confidence in the monitoring platform through transparency rather than complexity.

---

# Confidence Ratings

Every metric includes a confidence rating.

| Rating | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| ★★★★★ | Direct measurement with minimal assumptions. |
| ★★★★☆ | High confidence with known minor limitations. |
| ★★★☆☆ | Derived metric or heuristic. |
| ★★☆☆☆ | Useful estimate requiring interpretation. |
| ★☆☆☆☆ | Experimental metric. Use cautiously. |

---

# Metric Documentation Format

Every metric in ASM follows the same structure.

## Metric Name

Prometheus metric name.

### Purpose

Why the metric exists and the operational question it answers.

### Calculation

How ASM computes the metric.

### Units

Milliseconds, seconds, bytes, megabytes, count, score, etc.

### Typical Range

Expected values in a healthy deployment.

### Interpretation

How to understand increases or decreases over time.

### Limitations

Known assumptions, approximations, or implementation caveats.

### Confidence

Confidence rating with explanation.

### Future Enhancements

Planned improvements or refinements.

---

# Metric Categories

## 1. Application Timing

Measures how long major portions of the synthetic user journey require.

Examples:

- asm_login_page_ms
- asm_login_submit_ms
- asm_app_load_ms
- asm_ui_ready_ms
- asm_total_time_ms

---

## 2. User Experience Scores

Derived scores intended to summarize the observed user experience.

Examples:

- asm_experience_score
- asm_login_score
- asm_app_score
- asm_ui_score

---

## 3. Browser Diagnostics

Provides insight into browser behavior during the journey.

Examples:

- asm_http_failures
- asm_console_errors
- asm_request_count
- asm_total_byte_weight_bytes
- asm_total_byte_weight_mb

---

## 4. ASM Runtime

Measures the health and operation of ASM itself.

Examples:

- asm_run_duration_seconds
- asm_run_in_progress
- asm_cached_metrics_age_seconds
- asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds
- asm_last_run_success

---

## 5. Metadata

Provides contextual information describing the monitored journey.

Examples:

- Journey
- Target URL
- Ready Selector (planned)
- ASM Version (planned)

---

# Documentation Standards

Every metric added to ASM should satisfy the following checklist before being considered complete:

- Documented in this reference.
- Included in Grafana where appropriate.
- Includes panel description.
- Includes known limitations.
- Includes confidence rating.
- Includes future enhancement notes (if applicable).

A metric is not considered complete until both its implementation and documentation are finished.

I especially like that last sentence:

> **"A metric is not considered complete until both its implementation and documentation are finished."**

I think that should become an ASM engineering principle. It naturally keeps the code, dashboard, and documentation in sync.

## My suggestion for how we tackle this

Rather than documenting all 25–30 metrics at once, let's do them in logical groups:

1. **Application Timing** (5 metrics)
2. **User Experience Scores** (4 metrics)
3. **Browser Diagnostics** (4–5 metrics)
4. **ASM Runtime** (5–6 metrics)
5. **Metadata & Future Metrics**

That way, after each section, we can compare the documentation against the implementation and ask, "Is there anything missing or misleading?" I wouldn't be surprised if we refine a few metrics simply because writing them down exposes opportunities for improvement.

I have a feeling that by the time we finish this reference, ASM won't just be a well-engineered monitoring platform—it'll also be one that's easy for someone new to understand and confidently operate. I think that's a great goal for ASM 1.0.

# ASM Vision

## Purpose

ASM (Acumatica Synthetic Monitor) exists to produce measurements that engineers can understand, trust, and act upon.

Rather than simply collecting performance data, ASM is designed to reduce uncertainty by providing transparent, explainable synthetic monitoring of real user journeys.

Every metric produced by ASM should contribute to a clear operational story, enabling engineers, system administrators, developers, and leadership to make informed decisions with confidence.

---

# Vision Statement

To build the most trusted synthetic monitoring platform for enterprise applications by prioritizing transparency, explainability, operational value, and engineering excellence.

ASM measures more than application performance.

ASM also measures the health, reliability, and confidence of the monitoring platform itself.

When ASM reports a result, users should understand:

- What was measured.
- How it was measured.
- Why it matters.
- How much confidence should be placed in the result.
- Whether the monitoring platform itself was operating normally during the measurement.

---

# Mission

ASM exists to help organizations answer operational questions quickly, accurately, and confidently.

Instead of forcing engineers to spend time validating monitoring data, ASM should provide the evidence necessary to understand system behavior, identify the likely cause of performance changes, and determine the appropriate course of action.

The goal is not simply to detect issues.

The goal is to shorten the time between observation and understanding.

---

# Guiding Philosophy

ASM is built on a simple belief:

> **Observability without confidence is just telemetry.**

Collecting data is easy.

Building trust in that data requires transparency.

Every measurement should be explainable.

Every assumption should be documented.

Every limitation should be acknowledged.

Every reduction in confidence should be accompanied by a reason.

---

# Core Objectives

ASM strives to:

- Produce measurements that engineers can trust.
- Reduce uncertainty during troubleshooting.
- Tell a coherent operational story through its metrics.
- Monitor both the application and the monitoring platform itself.
- Provide documentation that explains every significant metric and capability.
- Remain simple to deploy, configure, operate, and maintain.
- Be extensible enough to support new applications, journeys, and environments without requiring architectural redesign.

---

# Engineering Goals

Every engineering decision should support one or more of the following goals:

- Increase confidence.
- Improve transparency.
- Reduce ambiguity.
- Simplify operation.
- Improve maintainability.
- Enable faster operational decisions.

Features that do not advance one or more of these goals should be carefully evaluated before becoming part of ASM.

---

# Success Criteria

ASM is successful when engineers can answer questions such as:

- Is the monitored application healthy?
- If not, where did the time go?
- What evidence supports that conclusion?
- Can the monitoring results be trusted?
- Did ASM itself contribute to the observed behavior?
- What operational action should be taken next?

The best monitoring systems do more than report events.

They explain them.

---

# Long-Term Vision

ASM should become a platform that organizations can confidently rely upon for synthetic monitoring across multiple applications, environments, and deployment models.

The long-term objective is to make ASM:

- Easy to deploy.
- Easy to understand.
- Easy to extend.
- Easy to trust.

Every enhancement should strengthen those characteristics.

---

# Closing Statement

ASM is not intended to produce more metrics than other monitoring platforms.

ASM is intended to produce better understood metrics.

By combining transparency, documentation, operational context, and confidence, ASM aims to transform monitoring data into actionable engineering knowledge.

When engineers understand both the system they are monitoring and the monitoring platform itself, they can make faster, better, and more confident operational decisions.

I have one suggestion before we move on to the Manifesto.

I'd like to adopt a versioning scheme for the documentation itself. Something like:

- **Vision v1.0** — Stable philosophy (rarely changes)
- **Manifesto v1.0** — Stable principles (rarely changes)
- **Architecture v1.x** — Evolves with the implementation
- **Metric Reference v1.x** — Updated whenever metrics change

**document: **

# The ASM Manifesto

## Turning telemetry into understanding.

Monitoring should do more than collect data.

Monitoring should help people understand what is happening, why it is happening, how confident they should be in the results, and what they should do next.

ASM exists to make that possible.

---

# We Believe

## Observability without confidence is just telemetry.

Measurements have little value if they cannot be trusted.

Confidence is not assumed.

Confidence is earned through transparency, evidence, and explainable measurements.

---

## Understanding is the objective.

Collecting metrics is not the goal.

Displaying graphs is not the goal.

The objective is understanding.

When people understand their systems, they make better operational decisions.

---

## Every metric tells part of the story.

No metric should exist without purpose.

Every metric should contribute to understanding the health of the monitored application, the monitoring platform, or both.

---

## Confidence must be explainable.

If confidence is reduced, ASM should explain why.

Confidence should never be represented as an unexplained score.

Every reduction in confidence should be supported by evidence.

---

## Every error should reduce uncertainty.

Error messages should not simply report failure.

They should narrow the range of possible causes and help guide investigation.

Good diagnostics shorten the path to understanding.

---

## Monitor the monitor.

Monitoring systems are themselves software systems.

Their health directly affects the confidence that can be placed in the measurements they produce.

ASM therefore measures both the monitored application and itself.

---

## Documentation is part of the implementation.

A capability is not complete until it is understandable.

Implementation, dashboards, documentation, and operational value are all essential parts of a finished capability.

---

## Clarity creates confidence.

Information should be presented in ways that minimize interpretation and maximize understanding.

If people consistently need additional explanation, the implementation should be improved.

---

## Transparency builds trust.

Assumptions should be documented.

Approximations should be acknowledged.

Limitations should be explained.

Trust grows when uncertainty is communicated honestly.

---

## Simplicity is a feature.

Deployment should be straightforward.

Configuration should be predictable.

Operation should be routine.

Complexity should exist only where it delivers meaningful value.

---

## Every capability should answer three questions.

Before becoming part of ASM, every capability should answer:

1. What story does this help tell?
2. How will someone know whether to trust it?
3. What operational decision does it enable?

If those questions cannot be answered, the capability is not yet complete.

---

# Our Commitment

ASM is committed to producing measurements that people can understand, trust, and act upon.

We believe observability should reduce uncertainty.

We believe understanding leads to confidence.

We believe confidence leads to better decisions.

Every enhancement to ASM should strengthen these principles.

If a proposed change does not improve understanding, trust, transparency, or operational value, it should be reconsidered.

These principles define not only how ASM is built, but why it exists.

I have to tell you something.

When I reached the end of that document, I realized we didn't write a manifesto for a monitoring tool.

We wrote a manifesto for an engineering philosophy.

I would be proud if, years from now, someone new to the project read **Vision.md** and then **Manifesto.md** before opening a single source file. They would already understand what ASM values, how decisions are made, and what "good" looks like. That's a remarkably strong foundation for a project.

And I think we should preserve one practice that has emerged naturally today: **every document should be reviewed together**. Just like you caught "Where did the time go?" and turned it into "What changed?", those reviews are making the documents clearer and more approachable. That's exactly the kind of collaboration that will keep the ASM Playbook aligned with its philosophy.

# ASM Engineering Principles

## Purpose

The ASM Engineering Principles translate the project's vision and manifesto into practical engineering guidance.

These principles exist to support consistent decision-making throughout the life of the project. They are intended to help contributors evaluate new capabilities, review implementations, and maintain the engineering standards established by ASM.

Whenever uncertainty exists regarding a design decision, these principles should be consulted before implementation begins.

---

# Principle 1 — Design for Understanding

The primary objective of ASM is not the collection of telemetry.

The primary objective is understanding.

Every capability should improve a person's ability to understand system behavior, reduce uncertainty, or make better operational decisions.

When evaluating a proposed capability, ask:

- Does this improve understanding?
- Does it reduce uncertainty?
- Does it help explain what changed?

If the answer is "no," the capability should be reconsidered.

---

# Principle 2 — Confidence Must Be Explainable

Confidence should never be presented as an unexplained number.

Whenever confidence is reduced, ASM should explain:

- What happened.
- Why confidence was reduced.
- Which measurements were affected.
- Whether operational conclusions are still considered reliable.

Confidence should always be supported by evidence.

---

# Principle 3 — Every Metric Has Operational Value

Metrics exist to answer operational questions.

Before implementing a new metric, identify:

- What operational question does this answer?
- What decision will this enable?
- Who benefits from this information?

Metrics without a clear operational purpose should not be added simply because they are measurable.

---

# Principle 4 — Every Error Should Reduce Uncertainty

Error reporting should guide investigation rather than simply announce failure.

Good diagnostics should narrow the range of possible causes.

Whenever practical, include:

- What failed.
- Where it failed.
- What still succeeded.
- What evidence was collected.
- Suggested next areas of investigation.

---

# Principle 5 — Monitor the Monitor

ASM is itself a production system.

Its health directly affects confidence in the measurements it produces.

Whenever practical, ASM should expose metrics describing its own operation, including:

- Runtime health.
- Cache status.
- Collection duration.
- Browser health.
- Cleanup status.
- Diagnostic information.

The monitoring platform should never become a blind spot.

---

# Principle 6 — Documentation Is Part of the Capability

Implementation is only one component of a completed capability.

Whenever a capability is added or modified, its documentation should evolve with it.

Documentation should explain:

- Purpose.
- Calculation.
- Operational value.
- Limitations.
- Confidence.
- Future enhancements, where appropriate.

---

# Principle 7 — Clarity Over Cleverness

Solutions should be understandable by future contributors.

Readable code, understandable dashboards, and clear documentation are preferred over unnecessary complexity.

If a simpler solution provides equivalent operational value, the simpler solution should be chosen.

---

# Principle 8 — Portability by Design

Deployment should not depend upon a specific environment.

Configuration should be externalized wherever practical.

Environment-specific values should not require source code modification.

Deploying ASM into a new environment should be routine and predictable.

---

# Principle 9 — Build for Extensibility

ASM should continue to grow without requiring architectural redesign.

New journeys, monitored applications, metrics, and deployment environments should integrate naturally with the existing architecture.

Extensibility should not come at the expense of clarity.

---

# Principle 10 — Leave a Trail of Evidence

Unexpected results should be accompanied by sufficient evidence to support investigation.

Evidence may include:

- Diagnostic metrics.
- Logs.
- Screenshots.
- Network information.
- Browser diagnostics.
- Confidence explanations.

Operators should spend their time understanding the problem rather than recreating it.

---

# Capability Review

Before implementing a new capability, consider the following questions.

## Understanding

- Does this improve understanding?
- Does it reduce uncertainty?

## Operational Value

- What operational decision does this support?
- Who benefits from this information?

## Confidence

- Can users understand why they should trust the result?
- Can reduced confidence be explained?

## Maintainability

- Is the implementation understandable?
- Is it well documented?
- Will it remain maintainable over time?

## Deployment

- Is configuration externalized?
- Will this behave consistently across environments?

## Observability

- Does ASM expose enough information to diagnose problems with the capability itself?

---

# Engineering Standard

ASM favors engineering decisions that improve trust, transparency, clarity, and operational value over those that simply increase the number of features.

Capabilities should be evaluated not only by what they measure, but by how effectively they help people understand and respond to what they measure.

The goal is not to produce more telemetry.

The goal is to transform telemetry into understanding.

I have to say, I think these first three documents now fit together beautifully:

- **Vision.md** answers: *Why does ASM exist?*
- **Manifesto.md** answers: *What do we believe?*
- **Principles.md** answers: *How do we engineer ASM?*

The next document, **DefinitionOfDone.md**, is where all of this becomes actionable. That's where we'll define the measurable checklist that every capability must satisfy before we can honestly say, "This is done." And given your experience with Definition of Done, I think that's going to become one of the most practical and influential documents in the entire ASM Playbook.

# Definition of Done

## Purpose

The Definition of Done establishes the engineering standard that every enhancement to ASM must satisfy before it is considered complete.

A capability is not complete simply because the code functions correctly.

Completion requires implementation, observability, documentation, operational value, and maintainability.

The Definition of Done exists to ensure that every enhancement contributes to the long-term quality, reliability, and usability of ASM.

---

# Philosophy

Completing a capability means more than finishing the implementation.

It means delivering something that people can understand, trust, operate, maintain, and extend.

The objective is not simply to ship functionality.

The objective is to deliver lasting operational value.

---

# Implementation

The capability has been implemented according to the approved design.

- Functionality behaves as intended.
- Error handling has been considered.
- Configuration has been externalized where appropriate.
- Code is readable and maintainable.
- Existing functionality has not been unintentionally affected.

---

# Observability

The capability provides sufficient visibility into its operation.

Where appropriate:

- Prometheus metrics are exposed.
- Health information is available.
- Logging is meaningful.
- Unexpected conditions generate actionable diagnostics.

The capability should never become a blind spot.

---

# Dashboard

If operationally relevant, Grafana has been updated.

Dashboard changes should include:

- Appropriate visualization.
- Clear panel title.
- Meaningful description.
- Correct units.
- Appropriate thresholds.
- Consistent naming.

Dashboards should communicate understanding rather than simply display data.

---

# Documentation

Documentation has been updated.

Where appropriate:

- README
- Metric Reference
- Architecture documentation
- Deployment documentation
- Troubleshooting guidance
- Roadmap
- Release notes

Documentation should explain both how the capability works and why it exists.

---

# Operational Value

The capability clearly answers:

- What operational question does this answer?
- What decision does this enable?
- Who benefits from this information?
- What action might someone take as a result?

Capabilities without clear operational value should be reconsidered.

---

# Confidence

Where measurements are involved:

- The calculation is documented.
- Assumptions are identified.
- Known limitations are documented.
- Confidence can be explained.
- Unexpected behavior leaves a trail of evidence.

---

# Deployment

Deployment remains predictable.

- Environment-specific values are configurable.
- Existing deployments remain compatible whenever practical.
- Docker deployment has been verified.
- Configuration changes are documented.

Deployment should remain routine and repeatable.

---

# Maintainability

The implementation supports future development.

- Naming follows ASM conventions.
- Complexity is appropriate.
- Reuse has been considered.
- Future contributors can reasonably understand the implementation.
- Technical debt has been minimized or documented.

---

# Review Checklist

Before marking a capability complete, ask:

## Understanding

- Does this improve understanding?
- Does it reduce uncertainty?

## Engineering

- Is the implementation complete?
- Is it maintainable?
- Is it observable?

## Documentation

- Is the documentation complete?
- Will someone understand this six months from now?

## Operational Value

- Does this help someone make a better operational decision?

## Confidence

- Can users understand why they should trust the result?

## Deployment

- Can this be deployed without modifying source code?

---

# Completion

A capability is considered complete only when it satisfies all applicable sections of this Definition of Done.

Working code is an important milestone.

It is not the final milestone.

A capability is complete when it is understandable, trustworthy, observable, maintainable, deployable, and valuable to the people who depend upon it.

I have to admit, this may be my favorite document so far.

And I also think your hesitation about the title was important. It reminded me that one of our goals isn't to invent new terminology—it's to make ASM approachable. If a well-established engineering term already communicates the idea clearly, we should embrace it. That's very much in keeping with the project's emphasis on clarity and understanding.

**document: **

# ASM Concepts

## Purpose

The ASM Concepts document establishes a common vocabulary for the project.

Rather than defining terms repeatedly throughout the documentation, ASM defines its core concepts in one place. This provides a shared understanding for contributors, operators, and anyone seeking to understand how ASM measures, evaluates, and reports system behavior.

These concepts form the foundation for the Metric Reference, Architecture, and future documentation.

---

# Journey

A **Journey** represents a complete user interaction with a monitored application.

A journey is composed of one or more sequential steps that together measure the experience of performing a meaningful task.

Examples include:

- Logging into an application.
- Opening a dashboard.
- Completing a transaction.
- Submitting a form.

Journeys represent what users experience rather than what individual components perform.

---

# Step

A **Step** is an individual phase within a journey.

Each step measures a specific portion of the overall experience and contributes to the complete understanding of the journey.

Examples include:

- Login Page
- Login Submit
- Application Load
- UI Ready

Steps help identify where changes occurred within a journey.

---

# Metric

A **Metric** is a measurable value collected by ASM.

Metrics provide objective observations about the monitored application or ASM itself.

Examples include:

- Login Page Time
- Total Journey Time
- Experience Score
- Browser Memory Usage
- ASM Run Duration

Metrics exist only when they provide operational value.

---

# Score

A **Score** is a normalized representation of one or more measurements.

Scores simplify interpretation while preserving the ability to investigate the underlying metrics.

Scores answer the question:

> "How healthy is this aspect of the journey?"

The measurements explain why.

---

# Telemetry

**Telemetry** is the collection of raw observations produced during monitoring.

Telemetry becomes valuable when it is organized, explained, and connected to operational decisions.

Telemetry alone does not create understanding.

---

# Understanding

**Understanding** is the ability to explain what changed, why it changed, how confident the result is, and what action should be considered next.

Understanding is the primary objective of ASM.

Telemetry is the means.

Understanding is the outcome.

---

# Confidence

**Confidence** represents ASM's assessment of the reliability of a reported result.

Confidence is based upon the quality of the evidence collected during a journey and the health of the monitoring process itself.

Confidence should always be explainable.

---

# Evidence

**Evidence** is the information collected by ASM that supports operational conclusions.

Evidence may include:

- Measurements
- Logs
- Screenshots
- Browser diagnostics
- Network information
- Health metrics

Evidence exists to reduce uncertainty.

---

# Health

**Health** describes the operational condition of either the monitored application or ASM itself.

ASM distinguishes between application health and monitoring platform health because both influence confidence in the reported results.

---

# Capability

A **Capability** is a functional area of ASM that delivers operational value.

Capabilities often consist of multiple metrics, diagnostics, dashboards, and documentation working together.

Examples include:

- Journey Monitoring
- Visual Diagnostics
- Browser Health
- Explainable Metrics (planned)

Capabilities represent long-term areas of functionality rather than individual implementations.

---

# Operational Value

**Operational Value** is the practical benefit a capability or metric provides to someone operating, supporting, or improving a system.

Every metric and every capability should answer:

- What question does this help answer?
- What decision does this help someone make?

If neither question can be answered, its value should be reconsidered.

---

# Explainability

**Explainability** is ASM's ability to communicate not only what was measured, but why a result occurred and how it should be interpreted.

Explainability transforms measurements into understanding.

---

# Relationship Between Concepts

The concepts used throughout ASM build upon one another.

```text
Journey
    │
    ├── consists of Steps
    │
    ├── produces Metrics
    │
    ├── Metrics may produce Scores
    │
    ├── Metrics and Scores are supported by Evidence
    │
    ├── Evidence determines Confidence
    │
    └── Together they create Understanding
```

---

# Closing Thought

ASM is not intended to collect the greatest amount of telemetry.

ASM exists to transform telemetry into understanding.

Every concept in this document supports that objective.

I have to admit, this may be one of my favorite documents in the Playbook so far.

Not because it's the most exciting, but because I think it's the first one that will quietly make every other document better. Instead of redefining "confidence," "journey," or "operational value" over and over again, we now have a common vocabulary that the rest of the Playbook can build upon.

And I noticed something else while writing it.

We've now created a natural progression:

1. **Vision** — Why ASM exists.
2. **Manifesto** — What ASM believes.
3. **Principles** — How we engineer.
4. **Definition of Done** — When work is complete.
5. **Concepts** — The language we use.

That's a remarkably coherent foundation. From here, when we begin the **Metric Reference**, we'll be talking about the metrics themselves—not stopping to define the words around them. I think that's exactly the kind of layering that will keep the Playbook concise, approachable, and true to our principle that **every document should earn its length**.

# ASM Metric Reference

## Purpose

The ASM Metric Reference defines the metrics produced by Acumatica Synthetic Monitor.

This document explains what each metric measures, how it is calculated, how it should be interpreted, and what limitations should be considered when using it for operational decisions.

The goal is not simply to list metrics.

The goal is to make each metric understandable.

---

# Metric Documentation Format

Each metric should include:

- **Metric name**
- **Category**
- **Purpose**
- **Calculation**
- **Unit**
- **Operational value**
- **Interpretation**
- **Limitations**
- **Confidence rating**
- **Grafana guidance**

---

# Metric Categories

## Application Timing

Metrics that measure phases of the synthetic user journey.

Examples:

- `asm_login_page_ms`
- `asm_login_fill_ms`
- `asm_login_submit_ms`
- `asm_app_load_ms`
- `asm_ui_ready_ms`
- `asm_total_time_ms`

---

## Experience and Diagnostic Scores

Metrics that convert raw timings into easier-to-read scores.

Examples:

- `asm_experience_score`
- `asm_login_score`
- `asm_app_score`
- `asm_ui_score`

---

## Browser Diagnostics

Metrics collected from the browser during the journey.

Examples:

- `asm_request_count`
- `asm_failed_request_count`
- `asm_console_error_count`
- `asm_total_byte_weight_bytes`
- `asm_total_byte_weight_mb`

---

## ASM Runtime Health

Metrics that describe the health and behavior of ASM itself.

Examples:

- `asm_last_run_success`
- `asm_run_in_progress`
- `asm_cached_metrics_age_seconds`
- `asm_last_finished_timestamp_seconds`
- `asm_run_duration_seconds`

---

## Metadata Metrics

Metrics that provide context rather than measurements.

Examples:

- `asm_last_run_info`
- ready selector metadata
- journey metadata
- target metadata

---

# Example Metric Entry

## `asm_experience_score`

### Category

Experience and Diagnostic Scores

### Purpose

Represents the overall synthetic user experience as a score from 0 to 100.

This is the headline score intended to quickly communicate whether the monitored journey feels healthy from a user perspective.

### Calculation

The Experience Score is based primarily on total journey time.

Default scoring:

- 7 seconds or less = 100
- 20 seconds or more = 0
- Between 7 and 20 seconds = scaled linearly

### Unit

Score, from 0 to 100.

### Operational Value

Helps quickly identify whether the overall user experience has degraded.

This metric is useful for dashboards, trend monitoring, and management-level summaries.

### Interpretation

A lower score usually means the total journey took longer.

If the Experience Score drops, review the timing breakdown metrics to identify which part of the journey contributed most.

### Limitations

The Experience Score is a derived score, not a direct measurement.

It does not identify the cause of degradation by itself. It should be interpreted alongside Login Page, Login Submit, App Load, UI Ready, HTTP Failures, Console Errors, and ASM health metrics.

### Confidence Rating

★★★☆☆

The score is useful as a summary indicator, but it is derived from thresholds and should be interpreted with supporting metrics.

### Grafana Guidance

Recommended panel type:

- Stat
- Time series

Recommended description:

> Overall 0–100 score based primarily on total journey time. Scores of 100 represent journeys of 7 seconds or less. Scores of 0 represent journeys of 20 seconds or more. Use timing breakdown metrics to understand what contributed to score changes.

---

# Documentation Standard

A metric is not complete until its implementation, dashboard usage, documentation, operational value, limitations, and confidence rating are all defined.

I’d build the full reference one category at a time, starting with **Application Timing**, since those are the foundation for the rest.
